title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 96 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 513–517 (Night 96, continuing directly from nights-95), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 96 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. Sharrukān, Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the vizier Dandān ride to the monastery with a hundred horsemen while the army marches on, unaware. Dhāt al-Dawāhī, still taken for a holy ascetic, has sent word by carrier pigeon to King Afrīdūn to lay ten thousand horsemen in ambush. At the monastery she has the monk Maṭrūḥanā killed, and the kings carry off its treasure; Tamāthīl never comes. On the way back the Muslims are trapped in a narrow mountain pass. They fight all day, and that night the 'ascetic', missing and feared dead, returns with the head of the great patrician. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ وَالتِّسْعُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu wa-al-tisʿūna
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth-and-ninetieth,
sentences.i: And when it was the ninety-sixth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ شَرْكَانَ وَأَخَاهُ ضَوْءَ الْمَكَانِ وَالْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ وَالْمِائَةَ خَيَّالٍ سَافَرُوا إِلَى الدَّيْرِ الَّذِي وَصَفَتْهُ لَهُمُ اللَّعِينَةُ ذَاتُ الدَّوَاهِي وَأَخَذُوا مَعَهُمُ الْبِغَالَ وَالصَّنَادِيقَ لِأَجْلِ حَمْلِ الْمَالِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna sharrukāna wa-akhāhu ḍawʾa al-makāni wa-al-wazīra dandāna wa-al-miʾata khayyālin sāfarū ilā al-dayri alladhī waṣafathu lahumu al-laʿīnatu dhātu al-dawāhī wa-akhadhū maʿahumu al-bighāla wa-al-ṣanādīqa li-ajli ḥamli al-māli
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that Sharrukān and his brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the vizier Dandān and the hundred riders journeyed to the monastery which the accursed-one Dhāt al-Dawāhī had described to them, and they took with them the mules and the chests for the sake of the carrying of the wealth.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Sharrukān, his brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān, the vizier Dandān and the hundred horsemen set out for the monastery that the accursed Dhāt al-Dawāhī had described to them, taking the mules and the chests with them to carry off the treasure.
sentences.n: The print has واخاة, a misprint for واخاه, corrected here. wa-akhāhu, “and his brother”, is accusative after anna like Sharrukāna before it. khayyāl, “rider, horseman”, carries the print's own shadda. wa-al-miʾata khayyālin puts the article on the numeral, as the last night's wa-al-miʾatu fārisin did.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ نَادَى الْحَاجِبُ بَيْنَ الْعَسْكَرِ بِالرَّحِيلِ فَرَحَلُوا وَهُمْ يَظُنُّونَ أَنَّ شَرْكَانَ وَضَوْءَ الْمَكَانِ وَالْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ مَعَهُمْ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمُوا أَنَّهُمْ ذَهَبُوا إِلَى الدَّيْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu nādā al-ḥājibu bayna al-ʿaskari bi-al-raḥīli fa-raḥalū wa-hum yaẓunnūna anna sharrukāna wa-ḍawʾa al-makāni wa-al-wazīra dandāna maʿahum wa-lam yaʿlamū annahum dhahabū ilā al-dayri
sentences.l: And when the morning dawned, the chamberlain called out among the army the departure, and they departed, and they were thinking that Sharrukān and Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the vizier Dandān were with them, and they did not know that they had gone to the monastery.
sentences.i: When morning came, the chamberlain proclaimed the march through the camp, and the army set off, believing that Sharrukān, Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the vizier Dandān were with them, and never knowing that they had gone to the monastery.
sentences.n: aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu, “the morning morninged”: the verb and its subject share a root, a common way of saying “when day broke”. nādā … bi-al-raḥīli, “called out the departure”: the verb nādā takes bi- for the thing proclaimed.

sentences.t: هَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِهِمْ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amrihim
sentences.l: This is what was of their affair;
sentences.i: So much for them.
sentences.n: The storyteller's formula for leaving one thread and taking up another; the next sentence, wa-ammā mā kāna min amri …, “and as for what was of the affair of …”, is its partner.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ شَرْكَانَ وَأَخِيهِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ وَالْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ فَإِنَّهُمْ أَقَامُو إِلَى آخِرِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri sharrukāna wa-akhīhi ḍawʾi al-makāni wa-al-wazīri dandāna fa-innahum aqāmū ilā ākhiri al-nahāri
sentences.l: and as for what was of the affair of Sharrukān and his brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the vizier Dandān, they stayed until the end of the day.
sentences.i: As for Sharrukān, his brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the vizier Dandān, they waited until the end of the day.
sentences.n: اقامو, aqāmū, “they stayed”, is spelt without the silent alif that Classical writing adds after the plural -ū; the print often drops it. After wa-ammā, “as for”, the answer is introduced by fa-, here fa-innahum, “why, they …”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتِ الْكُفَّارُ أَصْحَابُ ذَاتِ الدَّوَاهِي رَحَلُوا خُفْيَةً بَعْدَأَنْ دَخَلُوا عَلَيْهَا وَقَبَّلُوا يَدَيْهَا وَرِجْلَيْهَا وَاسْتَأْذَنَهَا فِى الرَّحِيلِ فَأَذِنَتْ لَهُمْ وَأَمَرَتْهُمْ بِمَا شَاءَتْ مِنَ الْمَكْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-kānati al-kuffāru aṣḥābu dhāti al-dawāhī raḥalū khufyatan baʿda an dakhalū ʿalayhā wa-qabbalū yadayhā wa-rijlayhā wa-istaʾdhanahā fī al-raḥīli fa-adhinat lahum wa-amarathum bi-mā shāʾat mina al-makri
sentences.l: And the infidels, the companions of Dhāt al-Dawāhī, had departed in-secret, after they had gone in to her and kissed her two hands and her two feet, and asked-her-leave for the departure; and she gave-leave to them, and commanded them with what she willed of the cunning.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the infidels who had come with Dhāt al-Dawāhī had already slipped away in secret. Before going they had come in to her, kissed her hands and her feet and asked her leave to depart; she gave it, and charged them with whatever trickery she pleased.
sentences.n: kānat … raḥalū, “were … had departed”: kāna with a past verb makes a pluperfect, “had already left”. The feminine kānat agrees with al-kuffār, a broken plural, while raḥalū goes back to the masculine plural. بعدان is baʿda an, “after”, printed as one word. واستاذنها is singular, “and he asked her leave”, among plural verbs; it may be the print's slip for واستاذنوها, “and they asked her leave”, but it is kept as printed and read as the band asking leave. amara bi-, “command (someone) with”: the verb takes bi- for the thing commanded.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَنَّ الظَّلَامُ قَامَتِ الْعَجُوزُ وَقَالَتْ لِضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ وَأَصْحَابِهِ قُومُوا مَعِي إِلَى الْجَبَلِ وَخُذُوا مَعَكُمْ قَلِيلًا مِنَ الْعَسْكَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā janna al-ẓalāmu qāmati al-ʿajūzu wa-qālat li-ḍawʾi al-makāni wa-aṣḥābihi qūmū maʿī ilā al-jabali wa-khudhū maʿakum qalīlan mina al-ʿaskari
sentences.l: And when the darkness fell-dark, the old-woman rose and said to Ḍawʾ al-Makān and his companions: Rise with me to the mountain, and take with you a few of the troops.
sentences.i: When darkness had closed in, the old woman rose and said to Ḍawʾ al-Makān and his companions, “Come with me to the mountain, and bring a few of the men with you.”
sentences.n: janna, of night or darkness, is “to cover, to fall”; it shares its root with jinn, the hidden ones. The narrator now calls her al-ʿajūz, “the old woman”, though the men still see an ascetic.

sentences.t: فَأَطَاعُوهَا وَتَرَكُوا فِي سَفْحِ الْجَبَلِ خَمْسَةَ فَوَارِسَ وَسَارَ الْبَاقُونَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْ ذَاتِ الدَّوَاهِي
sentences.tr: fa-aṭāʿūhā wa-tarakū fī safḥi al-jabali khamsata fawārisa wa-sāra al-bāqūna bayna yaday dhāti al-dawāhī
sentences.l: And they obeyed her, and they left at the foot of the mountain five horsemen, and the remaining-ones went between the two hands of Dhāt al-Dawāhī.
sentences.i: They did as she said, leaving five horsemen at the foot of the mountain, and the rest went on ahead of Dhāt al-Dawāhī.
sentences.n: bayna yaday, “between the two hands of”, here means in front of her as she leads them up the slope.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ عِنْدَهَا قُوَّةٌ مِنْ شِدَّةِ فَرَحِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra ʿindahā quwwatun min shiddati faraḥihā
sentences.l: And there came-to-be with her a strength from the intensity of her joy,
sentences.i: Such was her joy that strength came into her,
sentences.n: ṣāra is masculine though quwwa is feminine; when words stand between verb and subject, the verb often stays masculine.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ يَقُولُ سُبْحَانَ مَنْ قَوَّي هَذَا الزَّاهِدَ الَّذِي مَا رَأَيْنَا مِثْلَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra ḍawʾu al-makāni yaqūlu subḥāna man qawwā hādhā al-zāhida alladhī mā raʾaynā mithlahu
sentences.l: and Ḍawʾ al-Makān began saying: Glory to Him who has strengthened this ascetic, the like of whom we have not seen!
sentences.i: and Ḍawʾ al-Makān kept saying, “Glory be to Him who has given such strength to this ascetic! We have never seen his like.”
sentences.n: The print spells qawwā, “he strengthened”, with a final yāʾ (قوي) rather than alif maqṣūra; it is read as the form II verb. ṣāra yaqūlu, “became saying”, is “began to say, kept saying”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتِ الْكَاهِنَةُ قَدْ أَرْسَلَتْ كِتَابًا عَلَى أَجْنِحَةِ الطَّيْرِ إِلَى مَلِكِ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةِ تُخْبِرُهُ فِيهِ بِمَاجَرَى
sentences.tr: wa-kānati al-kāhinatu qad arsalat kitāban ʿalā ajniḥati al-ṭayri ilā maliki al-qusṭanṭīniyyati tukhbiruhu fīhi bi-mā jarā
sentences.l: And the soothsayer had sent a letter on the wings of the birds to the king of Constantinople, informing him in it of what-had-happened.
sentences.i: Now the soothsayer had already sent a letter on the wings of birds to the king of Constantinople, telling him all that had passed.
sentences.n: The soothsayer (al-kāhina) is Dhāt al-Dawāhī. kānat … qad arsalat, “had sent”: kāna with qad and a perfect gives the pluperfect. “On the wings of the birds”: by carrier pigeon. The print runs bi-mā jarā, “of what happened”, together as one word.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ فِي آخِرِ الْكِتَابِ أُرِيدُأَنْ تُنَفِّذَلِي عَشَرَةَ آلَافِ فَارِسٍ مِنْ شُجْعَانِ الرُّومِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat fī ākhiri al-kitābi urīdu an tunaffidha lī ʿasharata ālāfi fārisin min shujʿāni al-rūmi
sentences.l: And she said at the end of the letter: I-want that you-dispatch to-me ten thousands of horseman from the brave-ones of the Rūm,
sentences.i: and at the end of the letter she wrote, “I want you to send me ten thousand horsemen, the bravest of the Rūm,
sentences.n: The print runs urīdu an, “I want that”, together as اريدان, and likewise tunaffidha lī, “that you dispatch to me”, as تنفذلي. qālat, “she said”, is used of what she wrote. The Rūm are the Byzantine Greeks.

sentences.t: وَيَكُونُ سَيْرُهُمْ فِي سَفْحِ الْجَبَلِ خُفْيَةً لِئَلَّا يَرَاهُمْ عَسْكَرُ الْإِسْلَامِ وَيَأْتُونَ إِلَى الدَّيْرِ وَيَكْمُنُونَ فِيهِ حَتَّى أَحْضُرَ إِلَيْهِمْ وَمَعِي مَلِكُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَأَخُوهُ
sentences.tr: wa-yakūnu sayruhum fī safḥi al-jabali khufyatan li-allā yarāhum ʿaskaru al-islāmi wa-yaʾtūna ilā al-dayri wa-yakmunūna fīhi ḥattā aḥḍura ilayhim wa-maʿī maliku al-muslimīna wa-akhūhu
sentences.l: and their march shall be in the foot of the mountain secretly, lest the army of Islam see them; and they come to the monastery and lie-hidden in it until I come to them, and with me the king of the Muslims and his brother;
sentences.i: and let them march in secret along the foot of the mountain, so that the army of Islam does not see them. Let them come to the monastery and lie in ambush there until I come to them, bringing with me the king of the Muslims and his brother.
sentences.n: After urīdu an, “I want that”, strict grammar would carry the subjunctive on (wa-yakūna … wa-yaʾtū … wa-yakmunū); the print slips back into the plain indicative, wa-yakūnu … wa-yaʾtūna … wa-yakmunūna, and is vocalised as printed. wa-maʿī maliku al-muslimīna, “and with me the king of the Muslims”: a circumstantial clause, “while with me are …”.

sentences.t: فَإِنِّي خَدَعْتُهُمَا وَجِئْتُ بِهِمَا وَمَعَهُمَا الْوَزِيرُ وَمِائَةُ فَارِسٍ لَا غَيْرُ
sentences.tr: fa-innī khadaʿtuhumā wa-jiʾtu bihimā wa-maʿahumā al-wazīru wa-miʾatu fārisin lā ghayru
sentences.l: For I have-deceived the-two-of-them and come with-them, and with-the-two-of-them the vizier and a hundred horsemen, no other.
sentences.i: For I have tricked the pair of them and brought them here, and with them come only the vizier and a hundred horsemen.
sentences.n: jiʾtu bihimā, “I came with them”: jāʾa bi- is “bring”. lā ghayru, “not other”: and no more.

sentences.t: وَسَوْفَ أُسَلِّمُ إِلَيْهِمُ الصُّلْبَانَ الَّتِي فِى الدَّيْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-sawfa usallimu ilayhimu al-ṣulbāna allatī fī al-dayri
sentences.l: And I shall hand-over to them the crosses which are in the monastery.
sentences.i: I shall hand over to them the crosses that are in the monastery.
sentences.n: sallama ilā, “hand over to”. Who “them” are is left open: most naturally the horsemen she has just named, though it could be the Muslims, who have come for the monastery’s treasure. ṣulbān is a plural of ṣalīb, “cross”.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ عَزَمْتُ عَلَى قَتْلِ الرَّاهِبِ مَطْرُوحَنَى لِأَنَّ الْحِيلَةَ لَا تَتِمُّ إِلَّا بِقَتْلِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad ʿazamtu ʿalā qatli al-rāhibi maṭrūḥanā li-anna al-ḥīlata lā tatimmu illā bi-qatlihi
sentences.l: And I have resolved upon the killing of the monk Maṭrūḥanā, because the stratagem will not be-complete except by his killing.
sentences.i: I have made up my mind to kill the monk Maṭrūḥanā, for the plot cannot succeed unless he dies.
sentences.n: ʿazama ʿalā, “resolve upon”. bi-qatlihi, “by his killing”: by his being killed.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا تَمَّتِ الْحِيلَةُ فَلَا يَصِلُ مِنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ إِلَى بِلَادِهِمْ لَا دَيَّارٌ وَلَا نَافِخُ نَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā tammati al-ḥīlatu fa-lā yaṣilu mina al-muslimīna ilā bilādihim lā dayyārun wa-lā nāfikhu nārin
sentences.l: So when the stratagem is-complete, then there shall not reach, of the Muslims, to their lands, not a dweller and not a blower of fire;
sentences.i: Once the plot is done, not one of the Muslims will reach his own country again: not a living soul, not so much as a man to blow on a fire.
sentences.n: lā dayyārun wa-lā nāfikhu nārin, “not a dweller and not a blower of fire”, is a proverbial rhyming pair (dayyār / nār) for “no one at all”. The shadda of dayyār is ours; the print has none.

sentences.t: وَيَكُونُ مَطْرُوحَنَى فِدَاءً لِأَهْلِ الْمِلَّةِ النَّصْرَانِيَّةِ وَالْعِصَابَةِ الصَّلِيبِيَّةِ وَالشُّكْرُ لِلْمَسِيحِ أَوَّلًا وَآخِرًا
sentences.tr: wa-yakūnu maṭrūḥanā fidāʾan li-ahli al-millati al-naṣrāniyyati wa-al-ʿiṣābati al-ṣalībiyyati wa-al-shukru li-al-masīḥi awwalan wa-ākhiran
sentences.l: and Maṭrūḥanā shall be a ransom for the people of the creed, the Nazarene-one, and the band, the Cross-one; and the thanks to the Messiah, first and last.
sentences.i: and Maṭrūḥanā shall be a ransom for the people of the Christian faith and the company of the Cross. Thanks be to the Messiah, first and last.”
sentences.n: The pair al-millati al-naṣrāniyyati / al-ʿiṣābati al-ṣalībiyyati rhymes on -iyya. fidāʾan, “a ransom”: a life given up for the community. “Thanks … first and last” turns a familiar Muslim formula of praise toward the Messiah.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلَ الْكِتَابُ إِلَى الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةِ جَاءَ بَرَّاجُ الْحَمَّامِ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ أَفْرِيدُونَ بِالْوَرَقَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣala al-kitābu ilā al-qusṭanṭīniyyati jāʾa barrāju al-ḥammāmi ilā al-maliki afrīdūna bi-al-waraqati
sentences.l: So when the letter reached to Constantinople, the tower-keeper of the pigeons came to King Afrīdūn with the paper.
sentences.i: When the letter reached Constantinople, the keeper of the pigeon-loft brought the paper to King Afrīdūn.
sentences.n: barrāj, from burj, “tower”, is the keeper of the dovecote tower where the pigeons come home. The print puts a shadda on the mīm, which would make al-ḥammām “the bath”. The sense wants al-ḥamām, “the pigeons”, and the phrase is translated that way, but the printed mark is kept. jāʾa … bi-al-waraqati, “came … with the paper”: brought it.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرَأَهَا نَفَّذَ الْجَيْشَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَجَهَّزَ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ بِفَرَسٍ وَهَجِينٍ وَبَغْلٍ وَزَادٍ وَأَمَرَهُمْ أَنْ يَصِلُوا إِلَى ذَلِكَ الدَّيْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qaraʾahā naffadha al-jaysha min waqtihi wa-jahhaza kulla wāḥidin bi-farasin wa-hajīnin wa-baghlin wa-zādin wa-amarahum an yaṣilū ilā dhālika al-dayri
sentences.l: So when he read it, he dispatched the army from his moment, and equipped every one with a horse and a dromedary and a mule and provisions, and commanded them that they reach to that monastery.
sentences.i: As soon as he had read it, he sent the army out at once, equipping every man with a horse, a riding camel, a mule and provisions, and ordered them to make for that monastery.
sentences.n: min waqtihi, “from his time”: at once. jahhaza bi-, “equip with”. A hajīn is a swift riding camel.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلُوا إِلَى الْبُرْجِ الْمَعْرُوفِ كَمَنُوا فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣalū ilā al-burji al-maʿrūfi kamanū fīhi
sentences.l: And when they reached the tower, the known-one, they lay-in-ambush in it.
sentences.i: And when they reached the well-known tower, they lay hidden in it in ambush.
sentences.n: al-burj al-maʿrūf, “the well-known tower”: her letter named the monastery; the tower is presumably part of it or a landmark beside it.

sentences.t: هَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ هَؤُلَاءِ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri hāʾulāʾi
sentences.l: This is what was of the affair of these.
sentences.i: So much for them.
sentences.n: The storyteller's stock formula for switching from one party to another: “this is what there was of the matter of these … and as for …”.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ وَأَخِيهِ شَرْكَانَ وَالْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ وَالْعَسْكَرِ فَإِنَّهُمْ لَمَّا وَصَلُوا إِلَى الدَّيْرِ دَخَلُوهُ فَرَأَوُا الرَّاهِبَ مَطْرُوحَنَى قَدْ أَقْبَلَ لِيَنْظُرَ حَالَهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-maliki ḍawʾi al-makāni wa-akhīhi sharrukāna wa-al-wazīri dandāna wa-al-ʿaskari fa-innahum lammā waṣalū ilā al-dayri dakhalūhu fa-raʾawu al-rāhiba maṭrūḥanā qad aqbala li-yanẓura ḥālahum
sentences.l: And as for what was of the affair of King Ḍawʾ al-Makān and his brother Sharrukān and the vizier Dandān and the troop, then they, when they reached the monastery, entered it, and they saw the monk Maṭrūḥanā had come-forward to look-at their state.
sentences.i: As for King Ḍawʾ al-Makān, his brother Sharrukān, the vizier Dandān and their company: when they reached the monastery they went in, and saw the monk Maṭrūḥanā coming out to see who they were.
sentences.n: The print spells the monk's name مطروحنى here, with alif maqṣūra; it is the same Maṭrūḥanā. al-ʿaskar, “the troop”, is the hundred horsemen they took with them.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الزَّاهِدُ اقْتُلُوا هَذَا اللَّعِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-zāhidu uqtulū hādhā al-laʿīna
sentences.l: And the ascetic said: Kill this accursed-one!
sentences.i: “Kill this accursed man!” said the ascetic.
sentences.n: The “ascetic” is Dhāt al-Dawāhī in disguise, ordering the death of her own accomplice.

sentences.t: فَضَرَبُوهُ بِالسَّيْفِ وَأَسْقَوْهُ كَأْسَ الْحُتُوفِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍarabūhu bi-al-sayfi wa-asqawhu kaʾsa al-ḥutūfi
sentences.l: So they struck him with the sword and gave-him-to-drink the cup of the deaths.
sentences.i: So they cut him down with the sword and made him drink the cup of death.
sentences.n: kaʾs al-ḥutūf, “the cup of deaths”, a stock phrase for being killed; ḥutūf is the plural of ḥatf, death. The two halves chime: al-sayf / al-ḥutūf.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَضَتْ بِهِمُ الْمَلْعُونَةُ إِلَى مَوْضِعِ النُّذُورِ فَأَخْرَجُوا مِنْهُ مِنَ التُّحَفِ وَالذَّخَائِرِ أَكْثَرَ مِمَّا وَصَفَتْهُ لَهُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma maḍat bihimu al-malʿūnatu ilā mawḍiʿi al-nudhūri fa-akhrajū minhu mina al-tuḥafi wa-al-dhakhāʾiri akthara mimmā waṣafathu lahum
sentences.l: Then the accursed-woman went with them to the place of the vows, and they brought-out from it, of the rarities and the treasures, more than what she had described to them.
sentences.i: Then the accursed woman led them to the place where the votive offerings were kept, and they brought out of it more rare things and treasures than she had described to them.
sentences.n: al-nudhūr are vows, and so the gifts vowed to the monastery: its treasury of offerings. The narrator, who has just called her “the ascetic”, here names her for what she is.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَأَنْ جَمَعُوا ذَلِكَ وَضَعُوهُ فِى الصَّنَادِيقِ وَحَمَلُوهُ عَلَى الْبِغَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda an jamaʿū dhālika waḍaʿūhu fī al-ṣanādīqi wa-ḥamalūhu ʿalā al-bighāli
sentences.l: And after they gathered that, they put it in the chests and loaded it on the mules.
sentences.i: When they had gathered it all, they packed it into the chests and loaded it on the mules.
sentences.n: بعدان is the print's run-together spelling of baʿda an, “after (that)”, set as one word; it recurs in this night.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا تَمَاثِيلُ فَإِنَّهَا لَمْ تَحْضُرْ لَاهِيَ وَلَا أَبُوهَا خَوْفًا مِنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā tamāthīlu fa-innahā lam taḥḍur lā hiya wa-lā abūhā khawfan mina al-muslimīna
sentences.l: And as for Tamāthīl, she did not come, neither she nor her father, out-of-fear of the Muslims.
sentences.i: As for Tamāthīl, she never came, neither she nor her father, for fear of the Muslims.
sentences.n: لاهي is lā hiya, “not she”, printed as one word. Of course no Tamāthīl was ever coming: she was the bait in the crone's story.

sentences.t: فَأَقَامَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ فِى انْتِظَارِهَا ذَلِكَ النَّهَارَ وَثَانِيَ يَوْمٍ وَثَالِثَ يَوْمٍ
sentences.tr: fa-aqāma ḍawʾu al-makāni fī intiẓārihā dhālika al-nahāra wa-thāniya yawmin wa-thālitha yawmin
sentences.l: And Ḍawʾ al-Makān stayed in waiting-for-her that day, and a second day, and a third day.
sentences.i: Ḍawʾ al-Makān stayed on waiting for her that day, and the next, and the day after.
sentences.n: thāniya yawmin, “second of a day”, is the everyday way of saying “the next day”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ شَرْكَانُ وَاللَّهِ قَلْبِي مَشْغُولٌ بِعَسْكَرِ الْإِسْلَامِ وَلَا أَدْرِي مَا حَالُهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla sharrukānu wa-allāhi qalbī mashghūlun bi-ʿaskari al-islāmi wa-lā adrī mā ḥāluhum
sentences.l: Then Sharrukān said: By God, my heart is occupied with the army of Islam, and I do not know what is their state.
sentences.i: Then Sharrukān said, “By God, my heart is uneasy for the army of Islam; I have no idea how they fare.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَخُوهُ إِنَّا قَدْ أَخَذْنَا هَذَا الْمَالَ الْعَظِيمَ وَمَا نَظُنُّ أَنَّ تَمَاثِيلَ وَلَا غَيْرَهَا يَأْتِي إِلَى هَذَا الدَّيْرِ بَعْدَأَنْ جَرَى لِعَسْكَرِ الرُّومِ مَاجَرَى
sentences.tr: fa-qāla akhūhu innā qad akhadhnā hādhā al-māla al-ʿaẓīma wa-mā naẓunnu anna tamāthīla wa-lā ghayrahā yaʾtī ilā hādhā al-dayri baʿda an jarā li-ʿaskari al-rūmi mā jarā
sentences.l: Said his brother: Indeed we have taken this wealth, the great-one, and we do not think that Tamāthīl or other-than-her will come to this monastery after there happened to the army of the Rūm what happened.
sentences.i: His brother said, “We have taken this great treasure, and we do not think Tamāthīl or anyone else will come to this monastery, after what has befallen the army of the Rūm.
sentences.n: The print has فد, a misprint for قد, corrected here. انا is read innā, “indeed we”, which fits the plural verbs that follow; anā, “I”, would be possible only loosely. yaʾtī is masculine although Tamāthīl comes first: the verb agrees with “or anyone else”, a looseness of everyday speech. ماجرى is mā jarā, “what happened”, printed as one word.

sentences.t: فَيَنْبَغِي أَنَّنَا نَقْنَعُ بِمَا يَسَّرَهُ اللَّهُ لَنَا وَنَتَوَجَّهُ لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يُعِينُنَا عَلَى فَتْحِ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-yanbaghī annanā naqnaʿu bi-mā yassarahu allāhu lanā wa-natawajjahu laʿalla allāha yuʿīnunā ʿalā fatḥi al-qusṭanṭīniyyati
sentences.l: So it-is-fitting that we are content with what God has made-easy for us, and we set-out; perhaps God will help us to the conquest of Constantinople.
sentences.i: We had best be content with what God has granted us, and set off; it may be that God will help us take Constantinople.”
sentences.n: annanā naqnaʿu, “that we are content”, with an indicative verb, stands where Classical Arabic would say an naqnaʿa, “that we be content”. This is ordinary Middle Arabic, and you will meet it often.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَزَلُوا مِنَ الْجَبَلِ فَمَا أَمْكَنَ ذَاتَ الدَّوَاهِي أَنْ تَتَعَرَّضَ لَهُمْ خَوْفًا مِنَ التَّفَطُّنِ بِخِدَاعِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma nazalū mina al-jabali fa-mā amkana dhāta al-dawāhī an tataʿarraḍa lahum khawfan mina al-tafaṭṭuni bi-khidāʿihā
sentences.l: Then they came-down from the mountain, and it was not possible for Dhāt al-Dawāhī to oppose them, out-of-fear of the seeing-through of her deceit.
sentences.i: Then they came down from the mountain, and Dhāt al-Dawāhī could do nothing to stop them, for fear that her trickery would be found out.
sentences.n: amkanahu an …, “it was possible for him to …”: the person is the object, so dhāta is accusative. tataʿarraḍa lahum, “put herself in their way”, i.e. hold them back. al-tafaṭṭun bi-, “waking up to, seeing through”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ سَارُوا إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلُوا إِلَى بَابِ الشِّعْبِ وَإِذَا بِالْعَجُوزِ قَدْ أَكْمَنَتْ لَهُمْ عَشَرَةَ آلَافِ فَارِسٍ
sentences.tr: thumma innahum sārū ilā an waṣalū ilā bābi al-shiʿbi wa-idhā bi-al-ʿajūzi qad akmanat lahum ʿasharata ālāfi fārisin
sentences.l: Then they journeyed until they reached the gate of the pass, and behold, the old-woman had set-in-ambush for them ten thousands of horsemen.
sentences.i: They rode on until they came to the mouth of the pass, and there the old woman had laid an ambush of ten thousand horsemen for them.
sentences.n: al-shiʿb is a mountain pass or ravine. akmanat, “she had set in ambush”, is the causative of kamana, “lie hidden”, the verb used above of the troops lying hidden in the tower (kamanū): the troops she sent for are now in place.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَوْهُمْ أَحَاطُوا بِهِمْ مِنْ كُلِّ جَانِبٍ وَأَشْرَعُوا نَحْوَهُمُ الرِّمَاحَ وَجَرَّدُوا عَلَيْهِمْ بِيضَ الصِّفَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾawhum aḥāṭū bihim min kulli jānibin wa-ashraʿū naḥwahumu al-rimāḥa wa-jarradū ʿalayhim bīḍa al-ṣifāḥi
sentences.l: And when they saw them, they surrounded them from every side, and levelled toward them the lances, and bared against them the white of the broad-blades.
sentences.i: As soon as the horsemen saw them they closed in on them from every side, levelling their lances at them and drawing their white blades against them.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: al-rimāḥ / al-ṣifāḥ. bīḍ al-ṣifāḥ, “the white ones of the broad swords”, is the gleam of drawn steel.

sentences.t: وَنَادَى الْكُفَّارُ بِكَلِمَةِ كُفْرِهِمْ وَفَوَّقُوا سِهَامَ شَرِّهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-nādā al-kuffāru bi-kalimati kufrihim wa-fawwaqū sihāma sharrihim
sentences.l: And the infidels called-out with the word of their unbelief, and notched the arrows of their evil.
sentences.i: The infidels shouted out their creed of unbelief and nocked the arrows of their malice.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose again: kufrihim / sharrihim. fawwaqa is to fit an arrow's notch (fūq) to the bowstring.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ وَأَخُوهُ شَرْكَانُ وَالْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ إِلَى هَذَا الْجَيْشِ فَرَأَوْهُ جَيْشًا عَظِيمًا
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara ḍawʾu al-makāni wa-akhūhu sharrukānu wa-al-wazīru dandānu ilā hādhā al-jayshi fa-raʾawhu jayshan ʿaẓīman
sentences.l: And Ḍawʾ al-Makān and his brother Sharrukān and the vizier Dandān looked at this army, and they saw it an army great.
sentences.i: Ḍawʾ al-Makān, his brother Sharrukān and the vizier Dandān looked at this host and saw that it was a mighty army.

sentences.t: وَقَالُوا مَنْ أَعْلَمَ هَذِهِ الْعَسَاكِرَ بِنَا
sentences.tr: wa-qālū man aʿlama hādhihi al-ʿasākira binā
sentences.l: And they said: Who made-known to these armies about us?
sentences.i: And they said, “Who can have told these troops of us?”
sentences.n: aʿlama … bi-, “inform someone of”: the causative (form IV) of ʿalima, “know”, which takes the thing made known with bi-.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ شَرْكَانُ يَا أَخِي مَا هَذَا وَقْتُ كَلَامٍ بَلْ هَذَا وَقْتُ الضَّرْبِ بِالسَّيْفِ وَالرَّمْيِ بِالسِّهَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla sharrukānu yā akhī mā hādhā waqtu kalāmin bal hādhā waqtu al-ḍarbi bi-al-sayfi wa-al-ramyi bi-al-sihāmi
sentences.l: So Sharrukān said: O my brother, not this is a time of talk; rather this is the time of the striking with the sword and the shooting with the arrows.
sentences.i: Sharrukān said, “Brother, this is no time for talk. This is the time to strike with the sword and to shoot with arrows.

sentences.t: فَشُدُّوا عَزْمَكُمْ وَقَوُّوا نُفُوسَكُمْ لِأَنَّ هَذَا الشِّعْبَ مِثْلُ الدَّرْبِ لَهُ بَابَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-shuddū ʿazmakum wa-qawwū nufūsakum li-anna hādhā al-shiʿba mithlu al-darbi lahu bābāni
sentences.l: So bind-tight your resolve and strengthen your souls, because this mountain-pass is like the lane: it has two gates.
sentences.i: So steel your resolve and stiffen your hearts, for this pass is like a city lane, with a gate at either end.
sentences.n: al-shiʿb is a ravine or pass between mountains. A darb is a lane of a town quarter, shut at each end by a gate: the enemy can close both ends on them. qawwū, “strengthen”, is the imperative of form II qawwā; the print marks its shadda.

sentences.t: وَحَقِّ سَيِّدِ الْعَرَبِ وَالْعَجَمِ لَوْلَا أَنَّ هَذَا الْمَكَانَ ضَيِّقٌ لَكُنْتُ أَفْنَيْتُهُمْ وَلَوْ كَانُوا مِائَةَ أَلْفِ فَارِسٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥaqqi sayyidi al-ʿarabi wa-al-ʿajami lawlā anna hādhā al-makāna ḍayyiqun la-kuntu afnaytuhum wa-law kānū miʾata alfi fārisin
sentences.l: And by the right of the lord of the Arabs and the non-Arabs, were-it-not that this place is narrow, I would have annihilated them, even if they were a hundred thousand horsemen.
sentences.i: By the truth of the lord of Arabs and Persians, were this place not so narrow I would have wiped them out, though they were a hundred thousand horse.”
sentences.n: sayyid al-ʿarab wa-al-ʿajam, “the lord of the Arabs and the non-Arabs”, is the Prophet Muḥammad, and the oath is by his standing with God. al-ʿajam are the non-Arabs, above all the Persians. The print marks the fatḥa of wa-law, “even if”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ لَوْ عَلِمْنَا ذَلِكَ لَأَخَذْنَا مَعَنَا خَمْسَةَ آلَافِ فَارِسٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ḍawʾu al-makāni law ʿalimnā dhālika la-akhadhnā maʿanā khamsata ālāfi fārisin
sentences.l: So Ḍawʾ al-Makān said: If we had known that, we would have taken with us five thousand horsemen.
sentences.i: Ḍawʾ al-Makān said, “Had we known this, we would have brought five thousand horsemen with us.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ لَوْ كَانَ مَعَنَا عَشَرَةُ آلَافِ فَارِسٍ فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ الضَّيِّقِ لَا تُفِيدُنَا شَيْأً وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ يُعِينُنَا عَلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-wazīru dandānu law kāna maʿanā ʿasharatu ālāfi fārisin fī hādhā al-makāni al-ḍayyiqi lā tufīdunā shayʾan wa-lākinna allāha yuʿīnunā ʿalayhim
sentences.l: So the vizier Dandān said: If there were with us ten thousand horsemen in this narrow place, they do not avail us a thing; but God helps us against them.
sentences.i: The vizier Dandān said, “Had we ten thousand horsemen with us in a place as narrow as this, they would be of no use to us at all. But God will help us against them.
sentences.n: law … lā tufīdunā: Classical Arabic answers law with a past verb (la-mā afādatnā, “they would not have availed us”); the text uses the plain present, as speech does. The feminine tufīdu agrees with the numeral ʿasharatu, “ten”. shayʾan is printed شيأ, with the hamza set on the alif of the accusative ending instead of on a yāʾ seat before it (Classical شيئا).

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أَعْرِفُ هَذَا الشِّعْبَ وَضِيقَهُ وَأَعْرِفُ أَنَّ فِيهِ مَفَاوِزَ كَثِيرَةً لِأَنِّي قَدْ غَزَوْتُ فِيهِ مَعَ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ حَيْثُ حَاصَرْنَا الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةَ وَكُنَّا نُقِيمُ فِيهِ وَفِيهِ مَاءٌ أَبْرَدُ مِنَ الثَّلْجِ
sentences.tr: wa-anā aʿrifu hādhā al-shiʿba wa-ḍīqahu wa-aʿrifu anna fīhi mafāwiza kathīratan li-annī qad ghazawtu fīhi maʿa al-maliki ʿumara ibni al-nuʿmāni ḥaythu ḥāṣarnā al-qusṭanṭīniyyata wa-kunnā nuqīmu fīhi wa-fīhi māʾun abradu mina al-thalji
sentences.l: And I know this pass and its narrowness, and I know that in it are many wastes, because I have campaigned in it with King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān where we besieged Constantinople, and we used to stay in it; and in it is water colder than the snow.
sentences.i: I know this pass and how narrow it is, and I know there are many wild open stretches in it, for I campaigned here with King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān when we laid siege to Constantinople, and we used to camp in it. There is water here colder than snow.
sentences.n: mafāwiz is the plural of mafāza, the usual word for a waterless desert, which sits oddly in a mountain pass; Lane also gives “a place of safety”, and the vizier may mean open ground beyond the narrows where they could escape. The sense is uncertain. ḥaythu, properly “where”, is used here for “when”.

sentences.t: فَانْهَضُوا بِنَا لِنَخْرُجَ مِنْ هَذَا الشِّعْبِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَكْثُرَ عَلَيْنَا عَسَاكِرُ الْكُفَّارِ وَيَسْبِقُونَا إِلَى رَأْسِ الْجَبَلِ فَيَرْمُو عَلَيْنَا الْحِجَارَةَ وَلَمْ نَمْلِكْ فِيهِمْ أَرَبًا
sentences.tr: fa-inhaḍū binā li-nakhruja min hādhā al-shiʿbi qabla an yakthura ʿalaynā ʿasākiru al-kuffāri wa-yasbiqūnā ilā raʾsi al-jabali fa-yarmū ʿalaynā al-ḥijārata wa-lam namlik fīhim araban
sentences.l: So rise with us, that we may go out from this pass before the armies of the infidels grow-many against us and outstrip us to the head of the mountain and throw upon us the stones, and we did not gain against them any aim.
sentences.i: So come, let us get out of this pass before the infidel hosts swell around us and reach the mountaintop ahead of us and rain stones down on us, and we can do nothing against them.”
sentences.n: yasbiqūnā is yasbiqū, still governed by an, “that”, with -nā, “us”, attached. fa-yarmū is printed فيرمو, without the silent alif that Classical spelling writes after the plural ending (يرموا). wa-lam namlik: lam with the jussive normally denies the past; here it carries on the feared future, “and we would get no hold on them”. arab is “need, aim, object”.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذُوا فِى الْإِسْرَاعِ بِالْخُرُوجِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الشِّعْبِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhū fī al-isrāʿi bi-al-khurūji min dhālika al-shiʿbi
sentences.l: So they took-to the hastening with the going-out from that pass.
sentences.i: So they set about hurrying out of the pass.
sentences.n: akhadha fī, “take to, set about”. asraʿa bi-, “make haste with” a thing.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ إِلَيْهِمُ الزَّاهِدُ وَقَالَ لَهُمْ مَا هَذَا الْخَوْفُ وَأَنْتُمْ قَدْ بِعْتُمْ أَنْفُسَكُمْ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى فِي سَبِيلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara ilayhimu al-zāhidu wa-qāla lahum mā hādhā al-khawfu wa-antum qad biʿtum anfusakum li-allāhi taʿālā fī sabīlihi
sentences.l: So the ascetic looked at them and said to them: What is this fear, and you have sold your souls to God (exalted is He) in His path?
sentences.i: The ascetic looked at them and said, “What is this fear, when you have sold yourselves to God the Exalted, in His cause?
sentences.n: The “ascetic” is Dhāt al-Dawāhī in disguise, who has herself called up the ambush. Selling one’s soul to God echoes Qurʾān 9:111, where God buys from the believers their souls and their goods for the Garden.

sentences.t: وَاللَّهِ إِنِّي مَكَثْتُ مَسْجُونًا تَحْتَ الْأَرْضِ خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ عَامًا وَلَمْ أَعْتَرِضْ عَلَى اللَّهِ فِيمَا فَعَلَ بِي
sentences.tr: wa-allāhi innī makathtu masjūnan taḥta al-arḍi khamsata ʿashara ʿāman wa-lam aʿtariḍ ʿalā allāhi fīmā faʿala bī
sentences.l: By God, I stayed imprisoned under the earth fifteen years, and I did not object against God in what He did with me.
sentences.i: By God, I lay imprisoned underground for fifteen years, and never once did I quarrel with God over what He did to me.
sentences.n: iʿtaraḍa ʿalā, “object to, take issue with”.

sentences.t: فَقَاتِلُوا فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ فَمَنْ قُتِلَ مِنْكُمْ فَالْجَنَّةُ مَأْوَاهُ وَمَنْ قَتَلَ فَإِلَى الشَّرَفِ مَسْعَاهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qātilū fī sabīli allāhi fa-man qutila minkum fa-al-jannatu maʾwāhu wa-man qatala fa-ilā al-sharafi masʿāhu
sentences.l: So fight in the path of God: whoever is killed of you, then the Garden is his refuge (maʾwāhu); and whoever kills, then to honour is his course (masʿāhu).
sentences.i: So fight in the way of God. Whoever of you is slain, Paradise is his shelter; whoever slays, his road leads to glory.”
sentences.n: The print has ماواة, a misprint for ماواه, corrected here. The print has مسعاة, a misprint for مسعاه, corrected here. The pair rhymes, maʾwāhu / masʿāhu, a little flourish of rhymed prose to close the speech. The print itself marks the ḍamma of qutila, “is killed”, and the fatḥa of qatala, “kills”, to keep the two apart.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعُوا مِنَ الزَّاهِدِ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ زَالَ عَنْهُمُ الْهَمُّ وَالْغَمُّ وَثَبَتُوا حَتَّى هَجَمَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الْكُفَّارُ مِنْ كُلِّ مَكَانٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿū mina al-zāhidi hādhā al-kalāma zāla ʿanhumu al-hammu wa-al-ghammu wa-thabatū ḥattā hajamat ʿalayhimu al-kuffāru min kulli makānin
sentences.l: So when they heard from the ascetic this speech, there went-away from them the care and the gloom, and they stood-firm until the infidels rushed upon them from every place.
sentences.i: When they heard these words from the ascetic, their care and gloom left them, and they held their ground until the infidels fell upon them from every side.
sentences.n: al-hamm wa-al-ghamm, “care and gloom”, a rhyming pair. hajamat is feminine, agreeing with al-kuffār taken as a collective.

sentences.t: وَلَعِبَتْ فِي أَعْنَاقِهِمُ السُّيُوفُ وَدَارَتْ بَيْنَهُمْ كَأْسُ الْحُتُوفِ
sentences.tr: wa-laʿibat fī aʿnāqihimu al-suyūfu wa-dārat baynahum kaʾsu al-ḥutūfi
sentences.l: And there played in their necks the swords, and there went-round among them the cup of the deaths.
sentences.i: Swords played upon their necks, and the cup of death went round among them.
sentences.n: Sajʿ: suyūf/ḥutūf, “swords/deaths”. ḥutūf is the plural of ḥatf, death; “the cup of deaths” is the stock image of battle as a drinking-round at which each man is served his death. kaʾs, “cup”, is feminine, hence dārat.

sentences.t: وَقَاتَلَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ فِي طَاعَةِ اللَّهِ أَشَدَّ الْقِتَالِ وَأَعْمَلُوا فِي أَدَاءِ الْأَسِنَّةِ وَالنِّصَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-qātala al-muslimūna fī ṭāʿati allāhi ashadda al-qitāli wa-aʿmalū fī adāʾi al-asinnati wa-al-niṣāli
sentences.l: And the Muslims fought, in obedience to God, the fiercest of the fighting, and they set-to-work in the delivering of the spear-points and the blades.
sentences.i: The Muslims fought in God's service with the utmost fury, and laboured at the plying of spear and blade.
sentences.n: Sajʿ: qitāl/niṣāl. adāʾ, “delivery, discharge”, is an odd word here. The usual idiom is aʿmala … fī, “ply (a weapon) upon”, and the print's اداء may be a slip for الاعداء, “the enemies”: “they plied spear-points and blades upon the enemies”. The printed word is kept and read as it stands.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ يَضْرِبُ الرِّجَالَ وَيُجَنْدِلُ الْأَبْطَالَ وَيَرْمِي رُؤُسَهُمْ خَمْسَةً خَمْسَةً وَعَشَرَةً عَشَرَةً حَتَّى أَفْنَى مِنْهُمْ عَدَدًا لَا يُحْصَى وَجُمَلًا لَا تُسْتَقْصَى
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra ḍawʾu al-makāni yaḍribu al-rijāla wa-yujandilu al-abṭāla wa-yarmī ruʾūsahum khamsatan khamsatan wa-ʿasharatan ʿasharatan ḥattā afnā minhum ʿadadan lā yuḥṣā wa-jumalan lā tustaqṣā
sentences.l: And Ḍawʾ al-Makān began striking the men and felling the champions and throwing-off their heads five by five and ten by ten, until he wiped-out of them a number not to-be-counted and sums not to-be-reckoned-out.
sentences.i: Ḍawʾ al-Makān set to cutting down men and felling champions, sending their heads flying five at a time and ten at a time, until he had destroyed of them a number past counting and a host past reckoning.
sentences.n: Sajʿ: rijāl/abṭāl, then yuḥṣā/tustaqṣā. jandala is “throw to the ground” (from jandal, a rock). jumal, plural of jumla, “a sum, a total”: ʿadad and jumal together are a set pair for numbers too great to tally. رؤس is the edition's usual short spelling of ruʾūs, “heads”.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ كَذَلِكَ إِذْ نَظَرَ الْمَلْعُونَةَ وَهِيَ تُشِيرُ بِالسَّيْفِ إِلَيْهِمْ وَتُقَوِّيهِمْ وَكُلُّ مَنْ خَافَ يَهْرُبُ إِلَيْهَا وَصَارَتْ تُومِي إِلَيْهِمْ بِقَتْلِ شَرْكَانَ فَيَمِيلُونَ إِلَى قَتْلِهِ فِرْقَةً بَعْدَ فِرْقَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa ka-dhālika idh naẓara al-malʿūnata wa-hiya tushīru bi-al-sayfi ilayhim wa-tuqawwīhim wa-kullu man khāfa yahrubu ilayhā wa-ṣārat tūmī ilayhim bi-qatli sharrukāna fa-yamīlūna ilā qatlihi firqatan baʿda firqatin
sentences.l: And while he was thus, lo, he saw the accursed-woman, and she pointing with the sword toward them and strengthening them; and everyone who feared would flee to her; and she began signing to them for the killing of Sharrukān, so they would turn to his killing, band after band.
sentences.i: While he was so engaged, he caught sight of the accursed woman pointing her sword at them and urging them on. Every man who lost heart fled to her, and she kept signalling to them to kill Sharrukān, so that they turned upon him to kill him, one band after another.
sentences.n: The “he” who sees her is not named; it may be Ḍawʾ al-Makān, whose deeds have just been told, or Sharrukān, at whom the bands are sent. tūmī is Middle Arabic for Classical tūmiʾ, “she signs, beckons”, with the final hamza dropped. naẓara, “look”, takes a direct object here: “he saw her”. The crone is openly directing the Christians; the Muslims read her gestures otherwise, as the next sentences show.

sentences.t: وَكُلُّ فِرْقَةٍ حَمَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ يَحْمِلُ عَلَيْهَا وَيَهْزِمُهَا وَتَأْتِي بَعْدَهَا فِرْقَةٌ أُخْرَى حَامِلَةً عَلَيْهِ فَيَرُدُّهَا بِالسَّيْفِ عَلَى أَعْقَابِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kullu firqatin ḥamalat ʿalayhi yaḥmilu ʿalayhā wa-yahzimuhā wa-taʾtī baʿdahā firqatun ukhrā ḥāmilatan ʿalayhi fa-yarudduhā bi-al-sayfi ʿalā aʿqābihā
sentences.l: And every band that charged upon him, he would charge upon it and rout it; and there would come after it another band, charging upon him, and he would turn-it-back with the sword upon its heels.
sentences.i: Each band that charged him he met with a charge of his own and put to flight; then another would come on behind it, and he would drive that back on its heels with his sword.
sentences.n: ḥamala ʿalā, “carry upon”, is the regular verb for a charge in battle. radda ʿalā aʿqābihi, “turn back upon his heels”: drive back in retreat.

sentences.t: فَظَنَّ أَنَّ نَصْرَهُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِبَرَكَةِ الْعَابِدِ
sentences.tr: fa-ẓanna anna naṣrahu ʿalayhim bi-barakati al-ʿābidi
sentences.l: And he thought that his victory over them was by the blessing of the worshipper.
sentences.i: And he believed that he owed his victory over them to the holy man's blessing.
sentences.n: al-ʿābid, “the worshipper, the devout man”, is the narrator's other name for the disguised crone, beside al-zāhid, “the ascetic”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ إِنَّ هَذَا الْعَابِدَ قَدْ نَظَرَ اللَّهُ إِلَيْهِ بِعَيْنِ عِنَايَتِهِ وَقَوِيَ عَزْمِي عَلَى الْكُفَّارِ بِخَالِصِ نِيَّتِهِ فَأَرَاهُمْ يَخَافُونَنِي وَلَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ الْإِقْدَامَ عَلَيَّ بَلْ كُلَّمَا حَمَلُوا عَلَيَّ يُوَلُّونَ الْأَدْبَارَ وَيَرْكَنُونَ إِلَى الْفِرَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla fī nafsihi inna hādhā al-ʿābida qad naẓara allāhu ilayhi bi-ʿayni ʿināyatihi wa-qawiya ʿazmī ʿalā al-kuffāri bi-khāliṣi niyyatihi fa-arāhum yakhāfūnanī wa-lā yastaṭīʿūna al-iqdāma ʿalayya bal kullamā ḥamalū ʿalayya yuwallūna al-adbāra wa-yarkanūna ilā al-firāri
sentences.l: And he said in his soul: This worshipper, God has looked upon him with the eye of His care, and my resolve against the infidels has grown-strong by his pure intention; so I see them fearing me and unable to venture upon me; nay, whenever they charge upon me they turn the backs and lean to the flight.
sentences.i: And he said to himself, “God has looked upon this holy man with the eye of His favour, and his pure intent has strengthened my resolve against the infidels. I see them afraid of me, not daring to come at me; whenever they charge me, they turn their backs and take to flight.”
sentences.n: Sajʿ: ʿināyatihi/niyyatihi, then adbār/firār. inna hādhā al-ʿābida … naẓara allāhu ilayhi: the holy man is set first as the topic and picked up again by ilayhi, “upon him”. wallā al-adbār, “turn the backs”, is the Qurʾān's phrase for flight (Q 3:111). The irony is the narrator's: the “holy man” is the one sending the enemy at him.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَاتَلُوا بَقِيَّةَ يَوْمِهِمْ إِلَى آخِرِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: thumma qātalū baqiyyata yawmihim ilā ākhiri al-nahāri
sentences.l: Then they fought the rest of their day to the end of the daytime.
sentences.i: Then they fought on for the rest of the day until its close.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا أَقْبَلَ اللَّيْلُ نَزَلُوا فِي مَغَارَةٍ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الشِّعْبِ مِنْ كَثْرَةِ مَا حَصَلَ لَهُمْ مِنَ الْوَبَالِ وَرَمْيِ الْحِجَارَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā aqbala al-laylu nazalū fī maghāratin min dhālika al-shiʿbi min kathrati mā ḥaṣala lahum mina al-wabāli wa-ramyi al-ḥijārati
sentences.l: And when the night came-on, they put-up in a cave of that pass, from the muchness of what had befallen them of the calamity and the throwing of the stones.
sentences.i: When night came on, they took shelter in a cave in that pass, worn down by all the harm that had come upon them and the stones that had rained on them.
sentences.n: al-shiʿb is a pass or ravine between mountains: the Muslims have been caught in a defile, where the enemy can hurl stones down on them from above. wabāl is a heavy, ruinous misfortune.

sentences.t: وَقُتِلَ مِنْهُمْ فِي ذَلِكَ الْيَوْمِ خَمْسَةٌ وَأَرْبَعُونَ رَجُلًا
sentences.tr: wa-qutila minhum fī dhālika al-yawmi khamsatun wa-arbaʿūna rajulan
sentences.l: And there were killed of them on that day five and forty men.
sentences.i: Forty-five of their men were killed that day.
sentences.n: The verb qutila, “was killed”, is singular before its plural subject, the regular Classical order.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا اجْتَمَعُوا مَعَ بَعْضِهِمْ فَتَّشُوا عَلَى ذَلِكَ الزَّاهِدِ فَلَمْ يَرَوْا لَهُ أَثَرًا فَعَظُمَ عَلَيْهِمْ ذَلِكَ وَقَالُوا لَعَلَّهُ اسْتُشْهِدَ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā ijtamaʿū maʿa baʿḍihim fattashū ʿalā dhālika al-zāhidi fa-lam yaraw lahu atharan fa-ʿaẓuma ʿalayhim dhālika wa-qālū laʿallahu ustushhida
sentences.l: And when they gathered with one-another, they searched for that ascetic, and they did not see of him a trace; and that weighed-great upon them, and they said: Perhaps he has been martyred.
sentences.i: When they had gathered together, they searched for the ascetic but found no trace of him. This weighed heavily on them, and they said, “Perhaps he has died a martyr.”
sentences.n: The print has الراهد, a misprint for الزاهد, corrected here. ijtamaʿū maʿa baʿḍihim, “gathered with one another”, and fattasha ʿalā, “search for” (Classical fattasha ʿan), are both everyday usages. ustushhida, “he was made a witness”, is the passive of the verb for dying as a martyr (shahīd).

sentences.t: فَقَالَ شَرْكَانُ أَنَا رَأَيْتُهُ يُقَوِّى الْفُرْسَانَ بِالْإِشَارَاتِ الرَّبَّانِيَّةِ وَيُعِيذُهُمْ بِالْآيَاتِ الرَّحْمَانِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla sharrukānu anā raʾaytuhu yuqawwī al-fursāna bi-al-ishārāti al-rabbāniyyati wa-yuʿīdhuhum bi-al-āyāti al-raḥmāniyyati
sentences.l: And Sharrukān said: I, I saw him strengthening the horsemen with the signs of-the-Lord and commending-them-to-refuge with the verses of-the-Merciful.
sentences.i: Sharrukān said, “I saw him myself, putting heart into the horsemen with gestures inspired from on high and commending them to God's protection with verses of the All-Merciful.”
sentences.n: Sajʿ: rabbāniyya/raḥmāniyya. aʿādha, “commit to refuge”, here means to recite protective verses of the Qurʾān over the fighters. يقوّى is printed with final ى for ي, a habit of the edition.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُمْ فِى الْكَلَامِ وَإِذَا بِالْمَلْعُونَةِ ذَاتِ الدَّوَاهِي قَدْ أَقْبَلَتْ وَفِي يَدِهَا رَأْسُ الْبِطْرِيقِ الْكَبِيرِ الرَّئِيسِ عَلَى الْعِشْرِينَ أَلْفًا وَكَانَ جَبَّارًا شَدِيدًا وَشَيْطَانًا مَرِيدًا
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā hum fī al-kalāmi wa-idhā bi-al-malʿūnati dhāti al-dawāhī qad aqbalat wa-fī yadihā raʾsu al-biṭrīqi al-kabīri al-raʾīsi ʿalā al-ʿishrīna alfan wa-kāna jabbāran shadīdan wa-shayṭānan marīdan
sentences.l: And while they were in the talk, behold, the accursed-woman Dhāt al-Dawāhī had come-forward, and in her hand the head of the great patrician, the chief over the twenty thousand; and he had been a tyrant fierce and a devil rebellious.
sentences.i: While they were still talking, up came the accursed Dhāt al-Dawāhī, carrying in her hand the head of the great patrician who commanded the twenty thousand, a fierce and overbearing man and a rebellious devil.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-: the “behold” of surprise; the bi- only marks what appears. Sajʿ: shadīdan/marīdan. shayṭān marīd, “a rebellious devil”, is a Qurʾānic phrase (Q 37:7).

sentences.t: وَقَدْ قَتَلَهُ رَجُلٌ مِنَ الْأَتْرَاكِ بِسَهْمٍ فَعَجَّلَ اللَّهُ بِرُوحِهِ إِلَى النَّارِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad qatalahu rajulun mina al-atrāki bi-sahmin fa-ʿajjala allāhu bi-rūḥihi ilā al-nāri
sentences.l: And a man of the Turks had killed him with an arrow, and God hastened his spirit to the Fire.
sentences.i: A man of the Turks had killed him with an arrow, and God sped his soul to the Fire.
sentences.n: ʿajjala bi-, “hurry (something) on”: the verb takes bi- for what is sent.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الْكُفَّارُ مَافَعَلَ ذَلِكَ الْمُسْلِمُ بِصَاحِبِهِمْ مَالُوا بِكُلِّيَّتِهِمْ عَلَيْهِ وَأَوْصَلُوا الْأَذِيَّةَ إِلَيْهِ وَقَطَّعُوهُ بِالسُّيُوفِ فَعَجَّلَ اللَّهُ بِهِ إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-kuffāru mā faʿala dhālika al-muslimu bi-ṣāḥibihim mālū bi-kulliyyatihim ʿalayhi wa-awṣalū al-adhiyyata ilayhi wa-qaṭṭaʿūhu bi-al-suyūfi fa-ʿajjala allāhu bihi ilā al-jannati
sentences.l: And when the infidels saw what that Muslim had done to their master, they leaned with their whole upon him and made the harm reach to him, and cut-him-to-pieces with the swords; and God hastened him to the Garden.
sentences.i: When the infidels saw what that Muslim had done to their leader, they threw their whole weight upon him, did him every harm, and hacked him to pieces with their swords; and God sped him to Paradise.
sentences.n: Sajʿ: ʿalayhi/ilayhi. مافعل is set as one word, for mā faʿala, “what he had done”. The two hastenings, one soul to the Fire and one to the Garden, are set side by side on purpose.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلْعُونَةَ قَطَعَتْ رَأْسَ ذَلِكَ الْبِطْرِيقِ وَأَتَتْ بِهَا وَأَلْقَتْهَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْ شَرْكَانَ وَالْمَلِكِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ وَالْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malʿūnata qaṭaʿat raʾsa dhālika al-biṭrīqi wa-atat bihā wa-alqathā bayna yaday sharrukāna wa-al-maliki ḍawʾi al-makāni wa-al-wazīri dandāna
sentences.l: Then the accursed-woman cut-off the head of that patrician, and came with it, and cast it between the two hands of Sharrukān and the king Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the vizier Dandān.
sentences.i: The accursed woman had cut off that patrician's head; now she brought it and threw it down before Sharrukān, King Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the vizier Dandān.
sentences.n: atā bi-, “come with”, is “bring”: the verb chooses the bi-. bihā and alqathā treat raʾs, “head”, as feminine, though it is normally masculine; the text has it so. The names fall into a chime: Sharrukān, al-Makān, Dandān.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهَا شَرْكَانُ وَثَبَ قَائِمًا عَلَى قَدَمَيْهِ وَقَالَ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ عَلَى سَلَامَتِكَ وَرُؤْيَتِكَ أَيُّهَا الْعَابِدُ الْمُجَاهِدُ الزَّاهِدُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhā sharrukānu wathaba qāʾiman ʿalā qadamayhi wa-qāla al-ḥamdu li-allāhi ʿalā salāmatika wa-ruʾyatika ayyuhā al-ʿābidu al-mujāhidu al-zāhidu
sentences.l: And when Sharrukān saw her, he leapt standing upon his two feet and said: The praise be to God for your safety and the seeing of you, O worshipper, the striver, the ascetic!
sentences.i: When Sharrukān saw her, he sprang to his feet and said, “Praise be to God that you are safe and that we see you again, O holy man, warrior for the faith, ascetic!”
sentences.n: The narrator says raʾāhā, “saw her”, while Sharrukān, still deceived, greets a man: salāmatika with masculine -ka, al-ʿābidu. Sajʿ: ʿābid/mujāhid/zāhid.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا وَلَدِي إِنِّي قَدْ طَلَبْتُ الشَّهَادَةَ فِي هَذَا الْيَوْمِ فَصِرْتُ أَرْمِي رُوحِي بَيْنَ عَسْكَرِ الْكُفَّارِ وَهُمْ يَهَابُونَنِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā waladī innī qad ṭalabtu al-shahādata fī hādhā al-yawmi fa-ṣirtu armī rūḥī bayna ʿaskari al-kuffāri wa-hum yahābūnanī
sentences.l: And he said: O my son, I have sought the martyrdom on this day, so I began throwing my soul among the army of the infidels, and they stood-in-dread-of me.
sentences.i: “My son,” came the answer, “today I sought martyrdom. Again and again I flung myself among the infidel ranks, and they shrank from me in awe.”
sentences.n: fa-qāla, “he said”: in speech the crone is a man, and the narrator follows the disguise. ramā rūḥahu, “throw one's soul”, is to hurl oneself headlong into danger.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا انْفَصَلْتُمْ أَخَذَتْنِى الْغَيْرَةُ عَلَيْكُمْ وَهَجَمْتُ عَلَى الْبِطْرِيقِ الْكَبِيرِ رَئِيسِهِمْ وَكَانَ يُعَدُّ بِأَلْفِ فَارِسٍ فَضَرَبْتُهُ حَتَّى أَطَحْتُ رَأْسَهُ عَنْ بَدَنِهِ وَلَمْ يَقْدِرْ أَحَدٌ مِنَ الْكُفَّارِ أَنْ يَدْنُوَ مِنِّي وَأَتَيْتُ بِرَأْسِهِ إِلَيْكُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā infaṣaltum akhadhatnī al-ghayratu ʿalaykum wa-hajamtu ʿalā al-biṭrīqi al-kabīri raʾīsihim wa-kāna yuʿaddu bi-alfi fārisin fa-ḍarabtuhu ḥattā aṭaḥtu raʾsahu ʿan badanihi wa-lam yaqdir aḥadun mina al-kuffāri an yadnuwa minnī wa-ataytu bi-raʾsihi ilaykum
sentences.l: And when you separated, the zeal for you took me, and I fell upon the great patrician, their chief, and he was counted at a thousand horsemen; and I struck him till I sent-flying his head from his body; and none of the infidels was able to draw-near to me; and I came with his head to you.
sentences.i: When you drew off, I was seized with zeal on your behalf. I fell upon the great patrician, their chief, a man reckoned worth a thousand horsemen, and struck him until I sent his head flying from his body; not one of the infidels could come near me. And I have brought you his head.”
sentences.n: yuʿaddu bi-alfi fārisin, “he was counted at a thousand horsemen”: bi- gives the rate, what he was worth. ghayra is protective zeal, the passion to stand up for one's own. The lie is barefaced: the narrator has just told us that a Turk killed the patrician with an arrow. اخذتنى is printed with final ى for ي.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
